newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mixed ex-Paris US air cargo rates on buoyant exports.
newsitem.headline: Mixed ex-Paris US air cargo rates on buoyant exports.

text.p: The Paris-North America air cargo market continues to prosper on the back of buoyant French exports, reflecting a stronger dollar, a Reuters survey showed.

However, the recovery in rates is not uniform and is likely to be a long process as long as capacity is slack and fuel surcharges continue to be applied. Most carriers are not yet following a rate increase Air France introduced on March 1.

"While demand has strengthened and with it a slight, upward movement in rates, you won't find many airlines rubbing their hands at the prospect of a real improvement in yields," one market source said.

"We can confirm that we have increased rates to North America, a sector generating a good level of demand at present," an Air France Cargo official said declining to comment on the specific scale of the increases nor the other regions involved.
A survey of several of the airline's forwarder customers showed little movement in rates on North American routes and in one case, even a generous decrease.
"It perhaps more accurate to talk of a revision in Air France's rates to North America than a general increase," a Paris-based official of a major international forwarder told Reuters.

"Non-contractual tariffs applicable to occasional, small volume shipments may well have risen but as far as agreements covering sizeable, regular traffic are concerned, the trend is one of a significant cut in rates on a French franc/kilo basis."

The forwarder added: "For example, we recenty negotiated a double-digit decrease with Air France on ex-Paris rates to Chicago due to our status as a loyal customer and the airline's wish for us to remain so. This is more or less standard practice especially on translatlantic routes where capacity is in plentiful supply."
A smaller-sized Paris-CDG forwarder expressed no surprise at Air France's "special offers" to the bigger agents.
"It's established policy that Air France favours the big forwarding groups while offering an inferior standard of service to smaller ones," a spokesman for the forwarder said.

"From our point of view, North American rates are stable and have probably reached their floor price. The market outlook is positive but it is difficult to see rates rising given the current capacity situation and certainly not while fuel surcharges are maintained," he added.
One U.S. carrier, Delta, recently withdrew the surcharge.

The U.S. features prominently in Air France's recently-announced summer freighter programme which will add a fifth weekly stopover at Chicago from the end of the month with the return leg to Paris via Prestwick.
The carrier is also to add a second weekly all-cargo stopover in Los Angeles which will be part of an existing Mexico City service.

Air France will start plying the Paris-Atlanta route with ad hoc freighter flights from next month following demands from shippers and forwarders to provide a direct service to the U.S.' southern states.
American Airlines is raising ex-Paris cargo rates, effective May 5.

"The increases will probably vary between three and five percent depending on the destination and customer and will co-incide with the revision of our pricing structure," a Paris-based AA cargo official said.
"We had a very good last quarter of 1996 and demand has remained buoyant so far in 1997, with French exports faring well in the light of a stronger dollar," he added.
However, the majority of transatlantic belly-carriers remain prudent and have adopted a wait-and-see attitude on rates.

"We base our decisions on what the main player, namely Air France, is doing. If we are hesitating on increasing rates this probably reflects unclear market signals. Obviously, we want to increase rates but it's a delicate situation and we don't want to do anything which would threaten a recovery which dates back to last autumn."
Continental Airlines, which operates daily passenger services from Paris to Houston and New York-Newark has put off raising rates because of a recent plateau in market activity.

"January and February were very good months for us, even the beginning of March. However, over the past couple of weeks or so, things have become a little flat and has left us hesitating on upping rates. We are keeping an eye on Air France and the other belly carriers but for the moment it's the status quo."

Meanwhile, renewed market vigour on routes between France and Canada, saw Air Canada increase its Paris rates to Montreal, Toronto and selected destinations by 30 centimes/kilo from March 1. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+5017
